title: Orion Systems - POC scoping: Latency/Throughput SLOs & Measurement Plan
meeting_header: Recorded: 2025-11-04 15:30 UTC | Duration: 54m | Location: Zoom | Attendees: Ethan Cole (Redwood AE), Maya Liu (Redwood SE), Daniel Reyes (Orion VP Product), Aisha Khan (Orion Platform Eng), Liam O'Connor (Orion SRE), Priya Menon (Orion ML Eng)
summary: POC scoping focused on defining latency and throughput SLOs for Orion's user-facing assistant. Discussed TTFT vs TPOT definitions, target p95/p99 numbers, workload sizing, warm vs cold cache considerations, synthetic vs production load generation, and a measurement plan + timeline for a 3-week POC. Agreed next steps: Redwood to run initial benchmarks with Orion sample prompts, share benchmark harness and pricing, and schedule a controlled load test week-of 2025-11-17.
topics: Define p95/p99 targets appropriate for interactive assistant (TTFT p95 <= 250ms; p99 <= 600ms as starting point)
Throughput targets and request concurrency assumptions (RPS and tokens/s)
Measurement plan: synthetic load, production replay, warm vs cold starts, cache priming
Benchmarks: sequence length distribution, batching, KV/prefix caching, quantized model variants
POC timeline and success criteria: latency SLOs, 95/99 stability, error rates, cost per 1M tokens
transcript:
[00:00] Ethan Cole: All right thanks everyone for joining, we'll kick off, um, a quick agenda — go over SLOs, workload sizing, and the measurement plan for the POC. Maya from SE will walk through the benchmark approach.
[00:18] Daniel Reyes: Great, thanks Ethan. To give quick context, our assistant powers the support UI and a small customer-facing chat widget, about 12K monthly active users, peak concurrent ~120 sessions. Our primary concern is perceived latency.
[00:34] Maya Liu: Got it. Before we dive in, can you confirm current infra? Daniel: we're on GCP, using internal inference endpoints today, some on CPU, some GPU for heavy ops. We have a homegrown cache layer but it's not tuned for KV caching per se.
[00:50] Aisha Khan: And we have regulatory constraints — data residency in EU for EU customers, plus SOC2 in progress. We'll need to see audit logs and KMS integration for Private later.
[01:10] Ethan: Noted — we'll include security docs. For the SLOs, quick defs: we use TTFT "time to first token" — the latency from request arrival to the first token emitted. TPOT is time per output token (roughly token generation time after first token). That's important because TTFT impacts perceived responsiveness, TPOT impacts long responses and throughput.
[01:35] Liam O'Connor: So for an interactive assistant, TTFT is most critical. We care about p95 and p99. What are realistic targets?
[01:45] Maya: From other customers we've scoped, a starting baseline for a user-facing assistant is TTFT p95 <= 250ms and p99 <= 600ms on a hosted path; TPOT for continued tokens p95 ~ 20-30ms/token depending on model and batch. But these depend heavily on sequence length, model, and batching.
[02:05] Daniel: That p95 250ms is… ambitious. Our users accept up to 500ms, but lower is better. We can aim for 250ms p95 in POC but want to see cost tradeoffs.
[02:20] Maya: Exactly — we'll surface cost per 1M tokens for each config. Also we need to test with both warm runs (cache primed, KV hits) and cold starts. Cold TTFT can be multiple seconds if model needs cold loading or if autoscaling is involved.
[02:40] Ethan: For measurement, plan has three arms: 1) synthetic RPS ramp using Redwood's harness with your sample prompt set, 2) production replay of anonymized request traces (if you can provide), 3) targeted cold-start tests to exercise autoscaling behavior. We'll capture TTFT, TPOT, tail latencies, error rates, token throughput, and cost metrics.
[03:05] Priya Menon: We can provide a 24-hour anonymized trace and a representative prompt set with distribution of seq lengths. Sequence lengths: 60% short (<64 tokens), 30% medium (64-256), 10% long (>256).
[03:25] Maya: Perfect — that distribution will drive batching and kernel selection. We'll note model variants: base FP16, Q4/8 quantized variants, and a small distilled variant for cost tests.
[03:40] Liam: For TPOT and throughput, we also want to define expected concurrency. Peak concurrent sessions 120, average QPS ~8-12, peak 40-60 RPS during spikes. Can POC simulate that?
[03:55] Maya: Yes — our harness can replay traces with inter-arrival times, simulate user think-time, and reproduce concurrency patterns. We'll run a steady-state run for 30-60 minutes at target RPS and then spike tests to 2x and 3x.
[04:12] Ethan: On SLOs let's capture both steady-state and degradation SLOs. Steady-state TTFT p95 target 250ms, p99 target 600ms. For spike recovery we expect TTFT p95 <= 1.5s during autoscale windows and recovery to steady-state within N minutes — we should define N, maybe 3-5 minutes.
[04:32] Daniel: We want recovery within 3 minutes ideally. Also explicit success criteria: 1) Meet TTFT p95 target in at least 90% of steady-state runs, 2) p99 under the defined threshold, 3) error rate <0.5%, 4) cost estimate within our budget (we'll provide budget range).
[04:50] Maya: We'll operationalize that in the POC report. Measurement details: metric definitions and instrumentation — recommend Redwood's SDK hooks to emit trace ids and span starts so we can separate network vs model vs decode time.
[05:04] Priya: We can add trace ids. Question: how do you measure TTFT exactly? Do you include client-to-edge network latency?
[05:12] Maya: Good question. We measure TTFT at the Redwood edge: request arrival at our front-end to first token out. For production-level measurements we can also supply library instrumentation to measure end-to-end from your client; we'll capture both so you can see network contribution.
[05:28] Liam: Also need to account for prefix/KV cache behavior: if the user's previous context is cached, that should reduce TTFT. How will you emulate cache hit rates?
[05:37] Maya: We'll run scenarios with cache primed (we seed the KV cache with representative keys) and cache-miss scenarios. We'll parameterize hit rates — you can tell us expected session stickiness and TTLs.
[05:50] Daniel: Our session stickiness is about 42% across one session, TTL 30 minutes. We'll add that to the data share.
[05:59] Ethan: Timeline: week 0 (this week) — finalize prompts, provide traces, and access. Week 1 — Redwood runs initial microbenchmarks (single-node p95/p99, TTFT/TPOT baselines) and shares results. Week 2 — controlled load test with synthetic and replay, spike tests, cold-start experiments. Week 3 — analysis, cost modeling, and final POC report + recommended config. Does that align?
[06:24] Daniel: Yes, sounds reasonable. We need a detailed measurement plan doc and the harness so we can review tests.
[06:31] Maya: We'll share the benchmark harness repo link and a spreadsheet that maps scenarios to metrics. We'll also share sample config files for model variants and batching settings.
[06:40] Priya: On model selection — we need to test at least two model families: one higher quality (bigger) and one optimized for latency (quantized). Can you show the tradeoffs in output quality vs latency?
[06:51] Maya: Absolutely — we'll run a quality regression on a small eval set (ROUGE/BLEU-ish for your prompts, plus human spot checks) and tie any regression to cost delta. We'll surface examples where quantization hurts outputs.
[07:05] Liam: From an SRE standpoint, we also need observability — per-route percentiles, traces, token-level cost breakdowns, and retention of logs for 90 days for audit. Is that part of the POC?
[07:18] Ethan: We'll enable a trial retention config and include dashboards with per-route p50/95/99, error rates, concurrency, and token cost breakdowns. For SAML/KMS and full SOC2, that's part of Private/Dedicated discussions; for the POC we can provide redacted audit logs and KMS integration notes.
[07:36] Daniel: Ok. A few clarifying Qs — when you report p95, is that across requests or tokens?
[07:42] Maya: p95 TTFT is across requests (time-to-first-token). TPOT percentiles are measured per-token but we usually summarize with median token time and p95 token time across emitted tokens in the window.
[07:55] Priya: Measurement plan should call out warm-up periods for the measurement runs and removal of outliers like deployment restarts.
[08:03] Maya: Agreed — we'll use a 10-minute warm-up before capturing steady-state metrics and exclude the first N minutes of cold tests. We'll flag any infra restarts.
[08:12] Ethan: Let's capture success criteria again in a concise list so we have alignment.
[08:16] Daniel: I'll read ours: TTFT p95 <= 250ms steady-state, p99 <= 600ms; TPOT p95 <= 40ms/token; error rate <0.5%; recovery from spike within 3 minutes; cost must be within provided budget (TBD). If we hit these targets on your hosted offering we'll talk Dedicated sizing and SLA.
[08:33] Maya: That matches our notes. One more note: for small bursts we may recommend a burst capacity strategy (pre-warmed pool) vs pure autoscale depending on startup time. We'll show both in the report.
[08:47] Ethan: All right action items — we'll capture and assign. Any other questions?
[08:53] Liam: Nothing else from SRE. Looking forward to the harness.
[08:56] Daniel: Same.
[09:00] Ethan: Thanks all, we'll send the harness link, the initial benchmark plan, and schedule the load test for week of 2025-11-17.
[09:08] Maya: Thanks everyone.
[09:12] [end of recording]
